\chapter{Two Words for How Something Looks}
\label{ch:bonito-y-guapo}
\hlchaptermodality{399}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say bonito and guapo, and say how something or someone looks.}

Complete ES-C399-guapo: say how two things look, and say which you prefer.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bonito]{bonito — the same word made small twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C399-bonito}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{easy}, then \emph{difficult}. (\emph{Fácil}; \emph{difícil}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item buenos / buenas — the good you already own.
  \item favorito — whose \emph{-ito} was a false friend. This one is the real thing.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bo-NI-to}, three beats with the weight on the middle. The \emph{b} between vowels is soft — lips barely meet. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bonito} — \textquotedblleft{}pretty,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}nice.\textquotedblright{}

It is \textbf{bueno} with \textbf{-ito} on the end. And this time — unlike \emph{favorito} two lessons back — the ending really \emph{is} the Spanish diminutive, the one that turns \emph{casa} into \emph{casita}. Something like \emph{nicely good}.

\textbf{Latin had already done exactly this, with exactly this root.}

Latin \textbf{bellus}, \textquotedblleft{}pretty,\textquotedblright{} looks like a simple word. It is not. It is a worn-down form of an older \textbf{duenelos}, which was built on the same \textbf{bonus} — \emph{good} — with a small-and-fond ending on it. \emph{Bellus} was a diminutive that had forgotten it was one.

So the sequence runs:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bonus}, \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{};
  \item Latin shrinks it fondly $\to$ \textbf{bellus}, \textquotedblleft{}pretty\textquotedblright{} $\to$ Spanish \emph{bello}, and English \textbf{beauty}, \textbf{beautiful}, \textbf{embellish};
  \item Spanish, centuries later, reaches for \emph{bueno} and shrinks it fondly again $\to$ \textbf{bonito}.
\end{itemize}

One root, the same move made twice, a thousand years apart, in two languages.

A note on the fish: \emph{el bonito} is also a tuna, and the dictionaries do not agree that it is this word. Treat it as a separate entry rather than a pretty fish.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un pueblo \textbf{bonito}} — a pretty village;
  \item \emph{¡Qué \textbf{bonito}}! — How lovely!
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now call a thing pretty: \emph{bonito}. And you can tell a real \emph{-ito} from the borrowed one in \emph{favorito}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bonito}
  \item \emph{un pueblo bonito}
  \item \emph{¡Qué bonito!}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces make \emph{bonito}? (\emph{Bueno} plus the diminutive \emph{-ito}.) And what was Latin \emph{bellus}, before it meant \textquotedblleft{}pretty\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{A diminutive of the same bonus} — good, made small.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[guapo]{guapo — the word the dictionaries argue about}

\label{lesson:ES-C399-guapo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{difficult}, then \emph{pretty}. (\emph{Difícil}; \emph{bonito}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item bonito — said of things. This one is said of people.
  \item feo — the opposite, and you have met it already.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{GUA-po}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{u} after \emph{g} is pronounced here — \emph{gwa}, one slide, not two beats. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{guapo} — \textquotedblleft{}good-looking,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}handsome.\textquotedblright{}

Every other word in this chapter has an answer. This one does not, and that is what it is here to show you.

\textbf{The Academy's account.} The \emph{Diccionario de la lengua española} sends \emph{guapo} to Latin \textbf{vappa} — wine that has gone flat — which Romans also used of a man who had gone the same way: a \textbf{good-for-nothing}. The road offered is \emph{good-for-nothing} $\to$ \emph{swaggerer, bully} $\to$ \emph{handsome}.

\textbf{Corominas does not accept it.} In the standard etymological dictionary of Spanish, that sense-history is argued against — the steps do not join up well enough to carry the word.

So: two standard authorities, one ordinary everyday adjective, no agreement. The DLE prints its derivation as a flat single line with no hedge, and a reader who saw only that line would never know there was a question.

\textbf{What is not in doubt} is the recent end of the story. In Spanish, \emph{guapo} meant \textbf{bold, swaggering, showy} before it meant \emph{good-looking} — you can still hear that older sense in \emph{un guapo} for a tough or a braggart. The handsome meaning is the youngest thing about the word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un chico \textbf{guapo}} — a good-looking boy;
  \item \emph{una chica \textbf{guapa}} — a good-looking girl;
  \item \emph{¡Qué \textbf{guapa} estás!} — You look lovely!
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say how something looks — \emph{bonito} for a thing, \emph{guapo} for a person, and \emph{feo} for either — and say which you prefer. And you have met a word where the two dictionaries you would reach for disagree, which is a normal condition for a word rather than a failure of the lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{guapo}
  \item \emph{un chico guapo}
  \item \emph{una chica guapa}
  \item \emph{bonito, guapo, feo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Academy derive \emph{guapo} from, and who disagrees? (\emph{Latin vappa, flat wine} — and \emph{Corominas} argues against it.) Which sense of \emph{guapo} is older, \emph{bold} or \emph{good-looking}? (\emph{Bold}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
